_note: The keyboard map this session ships, and the single source of it. iarch-keybinds renders .config/hypr/generated/keybinds.lua from this file plus the differences a person has saved in ~/.config/iarch/keybinds.json, so a bind is written here or in that file and nowhere else. Until Part 5 the direction was the other way round -- tools/extract_keybinds.py read this record out of .config/hypr/keybind.lua -- and the reversal is the point: a report about a file cannot be edited, because the next extract overwrites the edit, which is why the Shortcuts page was read-only. Every spelling a bind here may use is recorded in data/design/keybinds.json against the pinned compositor, and iarch-keybinds check validates this file against that record rather than against an assumption.

migrated_from.source: the v1 extract of .config/hypr/keybind.lua, kept in git history
migrated_from.rewritten_note: Written in the lower-case spelling the v1 record used for the key part of a combination -- it spelled modifiers upper-case and some keys lower-case, so `SUPER + SHIFT + right` and `SUPER + tab` sat side by side. A key name resolves case-insensitively (src/keybinds/Resolver.cpp:58), so both spellings bind the same key; the record normalises on one rather than carrying two.
migrated_from.why_rewritten: Each reached for a pre-Lua dispatcher name through `hyprctl dispatch`, which on a Lua config is evaluated as `hl.dispatch(resizeactive 30 0)` and is not Lua. The replacements and their argument tables are in data/design/keybinds.json.
migrated_from.why_bound_here: SUPER + H, SUPER + SHIFT + H and SUPER + K were declared in the Lua and never bound, and v1 carried them with the status reserved so nothing would reassign them by accident. SUPER + H is the shortcut overlay this part exists to build, so it is bound; the other two stay reserved.

No compositor exists here, so no gap has closed, and two limits are written into the script rather than hidden: hl.config writes and cannot read a leaf back, so `toggle` remembers which way it went in a one-word file, and the change is runtime state that the next reload or relogin puts back. action.lua:
function()
    local window = hl.get_active_window()
    if not window then
        return
    end
    if window.floating then
        hl.dispatch(hl.dsp.window.move({ x = -30, y = 0, relative = true }))
    else
        hl.dispatch(hl.dsp.window.swap({ direction = "left" }))
    end
end
action.why_lua: Asks the compositor whether the focused window is floating and picks one of two dispatchers. The v1 bind answered the same question by running `hyprctl activewindow -j | jq -r .floating` through bash and grepping for the string true, which needed two external programs to ask a yes-or-no question the Lua API answers with a boolean field (LuaBindingsQuery.cpp:129-138, LuaWindow.cpp:101-102).

The row used to exec `pamixer -i 5` / `pamixer -d 5`, and no step of install.sh ever installed pamixer: the name appeared in no package array, so on a machine this repository built the key was dead and the only thing that said so was a shell's 'command not found'. It now runs scripts/iarch-audio.sh, which drives `wpctl set-volume @DEFAULT_AUDIO_SINK@ 5%+ -l 1.0` -- the limit is why a held key cannot walk the volume into amplification, since wpctl(1) says values may exceed 1.0 to amplify -- and the `repeating` flag is what makes holding the key step instead of firing once per press. wireplumber is the package that provides wpctl and install.sh now installs it. No PipeWire session exists here, so no volume has changed. TODO(verify) KB-07.

scripts/iarch-audio.sh runs `wpctl set-mute @DEFAULT_AUDIO_SINK@ toggle`, which is the form wpctl's own manual gives as its example (wpctl(1), SET-MUTE), and passes the exit status through rather than flattening it: 2 is 'could not connect to PipeWire' and 3 a command-specific error such as an object that was not found, and a caller that cannot tell those apart cannot say anything useful. No PipeWire session and no wpctl exist here, so nothing has been muted. The row carries no `repeating` flag on purpose: a toggle the compositor fires again while the key is held flips back and forth and ends wherever the release happened to land. TODO(verify) KB-07. The speaker side is @DEFAULT_AUDIO_SINK@, resolved at runtime to a node id, which is what lets one key work on whichever device is default instead of on an id that changes every boot.

The capture side is @DEFAULT_AUDIO_SOURCE@, which wpctl(1) lists under SPECIAL IDENTIFIERS as the current default capture device.

scripts/iarch-brightness.sh runs `brightnessctl set +5% --min-value=1`, and the floor is the reason the row is a script rather than a bare brightnessctl call: without --min-value the compiled floor is 0, because p.min is zero-initialised and only `-n` raises it (brightnessctl.c:146-150, and calc_value clamps to it at :402-403), so a key the compositor repeats while it is held walks the backlight all the way to a black screen. The `=` in --min-value=1 is not a style choice either: the option is declared optional_argument, so a separate word is never consumed and would be taken for the operation. Arch builds the package with `make ENABLE_SYSTEMD=1`, which is the build whose non-root `set` falls back to logind's Session.SetBrightness (brightnessctl.c:217-228 and :371-395), so the key needs no root, no setuid bit and no `video` group. No machine here has a backlight, so no level has changed. TODO(verify) KB-07.

The mirror of brightness.up and the same script, with the suffix form `5%-` rather than the prefix form `+5%`: brightnessctl's parse_value accepts the sign on either side, but a leading `-` would be read by getopt as an option. The --min-value=1 floor is what stops a held key reaching a black screen, and calc_value forces the delta to -1 when a non-zero percentage request would round to zero (brightnessctl.c:397-398), so the step can never be a silent no-op on a backlight whose maximum is small. No machine here has a backlight, so no level has changed. TODO(verify) KB-07.
